extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (educational institutions), Title IX coordinators, campus administrators, and legal/compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and regulatory requirements for adopting and operating Title IX grievance procedures, including protections for participants, appeals, notice requirements, and how grievance processes interact with other disciplinary processes. Focuses on §106.45 and §106.46 provisions in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on basing discipline solely on grievance outcome (§106.45(h)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may not discipline a party, witness, or other participant based solely on the recipient's determination whether sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.45(h)(5) maintains recipient discretion to discipline those who make false statements, including materially false statements made in bad faith, only if there is evidence independent of the determination whether sex discrimination occurred. The provision applies after a determination of sex discrimination is made and does not pertain to the factfinding phase. Evidence developed during the Title IX grievance process may be used in a disciplinary process so long as the discipline is not based solely on the outcome of the grievance proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection from discipline for consensual sexual activity connected to grievance participation (§106.45(h)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants in grievance procedures cannot be disciplined based solely on consensual sexual conduct that may be collateral to a Title IX complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation addresses concerns that discipline for collateral conduct violations (e.g., consensual sexual conduct) may create a barrier to participation in grievance procedures. Although many institutions may not discipline consensual sexual activity, some do; including consensual sexual activity within §106.45(h)(5) removes a potential barrier to information sharing and promotes full and accurate factfinding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible disciplinary proceedings for alleged false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may initiate disciplinary processes under their codes of conduct to address false statements when there is independent evidence beyond the grievance outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes this does not condone or encourage false reports; commenters provided no evidence of increased false reports. Threatening or instituting disciplinary proceedings under circumstances outlined in §106.71 could constitute retaliation under that section. The Department declines to require recipients to adopt specific policies (e.g., mandatory procedures, mandatory discipline, nondisclosure agreements) governing false statements as part of this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal parity requirement (§106.45(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to appeals of dismissals under §106.45(d)(3), a recipient must offer an appeal process that, at a minimum, is the same as it offers in all other comparable proceedings, if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complaints of sex-based harassment involving a postsecondary student, a postsecondary institution must also offer an appeal on the bases set out in §106.46(i)(1). Recipients retain discretion whether to offer appeals for other types of sex discrimination complaints, but may not exercise that discretion arbitrarily. Recipients may adopt additional appeal procedures (e.g., different bases or timeframe) provided they apply equally to the parties and are reasonably prompt; the final rule does not require a specific timeframe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional grievance provisions must apply equally to parties (§106.45(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional rules or practices a recipient adopts as part of its grievance procedures must apply equally to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department retained 'equally' rather than changing to 'equitably.' Identical treatment is not always required in implementation; recipients may account for individual needs (e.g., offering an interpreter or disability accommodation to only the party who needs it) and still satisfy the equal-application requirement. Recipients may use shared governance or collective bargaining to adopt additional provisions, and may have employee parties with distinct rights under such agreements, so long as the recipient complies with §106.45 and articulates consistent principles if procedures apply to some but not all complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of range or list of supportive measures and disciplinary sanctions (§106.45(l))
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must 'List, or describe the range of' supportive measures available to complainants and respondents and the possible disciplinary sanctions and remedies that may be imposed following a determination that sex-based harassment occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may choose either to list all possible sanctions or describe a range. If the Clery Act applies, the Clery-required list satisfies §106.45(l)(2) but recipients must supplement that list if they intend to impose additional sanctions for Title IX-covered conduct outside Clery's scope. A recipient may impose only disciplinary sanctions that are set forth in its list or described range, including sanctions imposed after a respondent has graduated. The Title IX Coordinator does not have authority to bring civil or criminal charges; recipients retain discretion over sanctions which may vary by recipient type, population, and applicable law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-employee fact-specific inquiry (§106.46(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party is both a student and an employee, a postsecondary institution must decide whether §106.46 applies by conducting a fact-specific inquiry considering whether the party's primary relationship with the institution is as a student and whether the alleged harassment occurred while the party was engaged in education-related activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfying either factor is sufficient (but not mandatory) for §106.46 to apply; the institution may consider additional factors it reasonably deems appropriate, including applicable Federal, State, or local law and collective bargaining agreements. If §106.46 does not apply, the institution must comply with §106.45. The final regulations do not preclude imposing adverse employment actions as disciplinary sanctions (e.g., administrative leave permitted by §106.44(i)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written notice of allegations requirements (§106.46(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Written notice of allegations must include specified elements such as a statement that the respondent is presumed not responsible until a determination is made, and must be provided to parties whose identities are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must assure parties that they will have an opportunity to present relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence to trained, impartial decisionmakers (the provision does not limit recipients to a single decisionmaker). Respondents must be given time to prepare for interviews — this is fair and part of reliable grievance processes. Recipients may delay notice when there is a 'legitimate concern for safety' (e.g., protecting a complainant alleging dating or domestic violence) but should document justification for any delay. The Department declined to require that an advisor be prohibited from also serving as a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptness and equity in grievance procedures (general procedural standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grievance procedures must provide for the prompt and equitable resolution of sex discrimination complaints, balancing timeliness with fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing equity with promptness has been a Title IX requirement since 1975 (34 CFR 106.8(c)); promptness serves the nondiscrimination mandate by avoiding unnecessary delay. The final regulations preserve recipient discretion to set reasonably prompt timeframes for appeals and grievance steps, subject to the requirement that procedures be prompt and equitable and not applied arbitrarily.
